evidence: src/presentation/controllers/AppointmentsController.ts: constructor(private readonly scheduling: SchedulingService, private readonly notes: VisitNotesService) wires in business-layer services, which this layer is allowed to depend on.
book(form: BookingForm): converts new Date(form.startsAt), passes the call to this.scheduling.book(...), then returns present(appointment). This is translation plus delegation, with no rule logic.
cancel(id): present(await this.scheduling.cancel(id, new Date())) only passes the current time on to the domain service.
addNote(id, form): calls this.notes.write(...) and returns { count: (await this.notes.notesFor(id)).length }, a projection for the response rather than a domain decision.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This file fits the presentation layer. It declares input form shapes (BookingForm, NoteForm) and a controller. The controller's constructor takes two business-layer services, which counts as normal dependency wiring because presentation may depend on business. Each method only translates input: it turns the startsAt string into a Date, or supplies the current time as the cancel timestamp. It then hands the work to SchedulingService or VisitNotesService and formats the result with the presentation-layer presenter. Nothing in it is a domain invariant, calculation or decision. Booking checks, cancellation rules and note handling all live in the business services. Returning the number of notes is a projection for the response, not a business rule. No candidate flags were raised, and I found nothing extra in the source.
